newsitem.title: THAILAND: FEATURE - Police crack down on one night in Bangkok.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Police crack down on one night in Bangkok.

text.p: One night in Bangkok isn't as long as it used to be if you're out looking for a good time.
Part of the new government's answer to a soaring drugs problem is the slapping of a 3 a.m. closing time on many of the Thai capital's raunchy go-go bars, clubs and pubs.

In a city where police traditionally turn a blind eye to enforcing licensing hours, bar owners say the crackdown -- which has also seen police searching venues, customers and cars -- threatens Bangkok's reputation for a good night out.
"I think it's a bit of a shame because Bangkok is not quite as much fun as it used to be," said a bar manager in the city's world-famous Patpong girlie-bar strip where almost anything goes.
"I can understand it Monday to Thursday but we've asked the police to go easy on Friday and Saturday but they say they can't," he said.
AMPHETAMINE SEIZURES SOAR
Governments have in the past clamped down on the excesses of the entertainment industry, but usually such campaigns lost steam after a week or two, the bar manager said.

The current crackdown, already two months old, and what analysts say is popular support for Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's pledge to make 1997 a drugs-free year, have led many to conclude the police vigilance could go on indefinitely.
The crackdown followed a number of high profile drug crimes and came amid a perceived rise in drug use, particularly with amphetamines.
Ampethamine seizures between January and November 1996 totalled 470 kg (1,034 lb), eclipsing the 301 kg of heroin picked up in the same period for the first time since records began 20 years ago.

Police arrested nearly 95,000 people for narcotics related offences in the first 11 months of 1996, against 142,541 in 1995, but amphetamine related cases accounted for 32 percent of that total, against 14 percent in 1995.
VOTE-WINNING ISSUE

Against that background, the government stumbled upon a political gold mine when police killed six suspected drug traffickers in what they said was a shoot-out in provincial Suphan Buri in early December, analysts said.

Chavalit's subsequent comment that the police were doing their jobs, more police shootings of suspected traffickers and a comparison of the dangers of drugs in Thailand to the communist insurgency of the 1970s, were well received by voters, analysts said.

"I think this (issue) came to the administration by accident with the events in Suphan Buri... and with it they found a vote winning issue. This was one thing you can do to give you popularity fast," said Prathoomporn Vajrasthira, associate professor of political science at Chulalongkorn University.
Raiding and closing nightspots in Bangkok, where Chavalit's New Aspiration Party holds a single seat, ensured good publicity and minimal political damage, she said.

In what has been seen as an unprecedented degree of cooperation between the government and the police, Deputy Interior Minister Chalerm Yoobamrung, a former police captain, has created an anti-drug police squad and is closely supervising operations.

"To this extent I can't remember a precedent, at least not with this degree of cooperation with the police working hand in hand with the government... also it means the government can better direct the role of investigations," Prathoomporn said.
DWINDLING CUSTOMERS
But the clampdown on the Friday and Saturday night revellers has many suspecting that while the small fry are being caught, the bigger fish slip away.

"The government is doing this because it knows it will win popularity with some people, but I think it hits the consumers, not the suppliers," said a bar manager in Silom Road's fasionable Soi (lane) 4.
While determined revellers can still find a drink after closing hours in a few select locations, owners of many clubs subjected to police searches have watched customer numbers dwindle.
"Sometimes the police bring (sniffer) dogs into the club, all over the club," said a manager at the exclusive Taurus entertaiment complex near central Sukhumvit Road.
"We have a lot of high society people in the club so when that happens business is very seriously down because it makes trouble with our customers," he said.
